passages.title: Say what you do, and fight in solid ranks
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat are an answer to a question the Companions were too shy to ask out loud: *which deed is dearest to Allah?* Allah answers them — but before He does, He corrects the way they asked. The passage moves in one sweep: all creation glorifies its Lord (ayah 1), then believers are asked why they say what they do not do (ayat 2–3), and then comes the answer they wanted (ayah 4) — the deed He loves is fighting in His path, in ranks locked together like a single wall.

## The question behind the surah

Ibn Kathir records that Imam Ahmad transmitted from 'Abdullah bin Salam: "We asked, 'Who among us should go to the Messenger ﷺ and ask him about the dearest actions to Allah?' None among us volunteered. The Messenger ﷺ sent a man to us and that man gathered us and recited this Surah, Surat As-Saff, in its entirety."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills the scene in. Tirmidhi has recorded, on the authority of Sayyidnā 'Abdullah Ibn Salām, that a group of Companions discussed among themselves that if they came to know which action is dearest in the sight of Allah, they would act upon it; Hakim reported this tradition and graded its chain as sahih. Baghawi's citation adds the sentence that turns out to be the hinge of the whole passage: *"If we come to know which is the dearest of actions in the sight of Allah, we shall dedicate our lives and wealth to it."*

Ibn Kathir's version — with reference to the Musnad of Ahmad — tells us that while this discussion was still going on, and no one dared take the question to him ﷺ, the Prophet ﷺ sent a man to call each of them by name. When they all arrived, he recited to them the entire Surah As-Saff, which had been revealed just then.

Sit with that for a moment. They talked it over privately; nobody was brave enough to go and ask. And revelation came down naming their conversation, answering it, and correcting it — all before a word was spoken to him ﷺ. The answer they were looking for, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, is jihād in the cause of Allah.

But notice what came first. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that their statement — "if we come to know about it, we shall dedicate our lives to acting upon it" — was a sort of claim to having the ability to do it. And it is not proper for any believer to make such a claim, "because no one can for sure know whether he will be able to implement his intentions when the time arrives." It is not in a person's power that all the causes of action be made effective and all obstacles removed; nor are the abilities and strengths of his own hands and limbs altogether in his power; nor is his determination or intention completely in his control. This is why, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, even the Prophet ﷺ was instructed in the Qur'an: *"And never say about anything, 'I am going to do this tomorrow,' unless [you say] 'if Allah wills'"* (18:23–24).

The Companions' intention, it says plainly, was not to make a boastful claim — but it did seem apparently as a claim, which Allah dislikes. So ayat 2 and 3 come as the admonition, and ayah 4 as the answer.

## Ayah 1: the rebuke set against a background of praise

The surah opens with whatsoever is in the heavens and whatsoever is on the earth glorifying Allah — "and He is the Almighty (*al-'Azīz*), the All-Wise (*al-Hakīm*)." Ibn Kathir passes over this quickly: he notes that he has explained the meaning of this opening statement in many places before, and so does not need to repeat it here.

What is worth noticing is simply the order. Before the believers are asked why their words outrun their deeds, the passage sets them inside a creation that is glorifying its Lord. The rebuke that follows arrives inside that frame, not outside it.

## Ayat 2–3: why do you say what you do not do?

Ayah 2 comes as a question, not a verdict: *"O you who believe! Why do you say that which you do not do?"* And it is addressed to believers — "O you who believe" — people whose faith is affirmed in the very words that examine their speech.

Ayah 3 then names the weight of it: *"Most hateful it is with Allah that you say that which you do not do."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the same ayah, "It is severely hateful in Allah's sight that you say what you do not do." Both renderings carry the same emphasis: this is not listed as a minor slip.

**The Salaf on keeping promises.** Ibn Kathir says this ayah "refutes those who neglect to fulfill their promises," and that it supports the view held by several scholars of the Salaf: that it is necessary to fulfil a promise, regardless of whether the promise includes some type of wealth for the person receiving it or not. They also argue from the Sunnah, with the hadith recorded in the Two Sahihs in which Allah's Messenger ﷺ said:

> "There are three signs for a hypocrite: when he promises, he breaks his promise; when he speaks, he lies; and when he is entrusted, he betrays."

And with another hadith in the Sahih: "There are four characteristics which if one has all of them, he is the pure hypocrite, and if anyone has any of them, he has a characteristic of hypocrisy, until he abandons it" — among which the Prophet ﷺ mentioned breaking a promise. Read alongside ayah 3, the point is sobering: an unkept word is not a small social failing. It sits among the very traits the Prophet ﷺ named as signs of hypocrisy.

**Even a promise to a child.** Ibn Kathir then reports what Imam Ahmad and Abu Dawud recorded from 'Abdullah bin 'Amir bin Rabi'ah, who was a young boy at the time. Allah's Messenger ﷺ came to them, and 'Abdullah went out to play. His mother called him: "O 'Abdullah! Come, I want to give you something." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ asked her, "What did you want to give him?" She said, "Dates." He said: *"If you had not given them to him, it would have been written as a lie in your record."*

A handful of dates, promised to a small boy in his own house — and the Prophet ﷺ tells the mother it would have been written against her as a lie. Whatever else these ayat mean, they mean this: what we say to the people closest to us is written down.

**Which words, exactly?** The commentators report more than one situation the rebuke addressed, and Ibn Kathir preserves them side by side.

Muqatil bin Hayyan said the faithful believers had declared, "If we only knew the dearest good actions to Allah, we would perform them" — so Allah told them about the dearest actions to Him, "Verily, Allah loves those who fight in His cause in rows." Allah stated what He likes, "and they were tested on the day of Uhud. However, they retreated and fled, leaving the Prophet ﷺ behind," and it was about their case that Allah revealed *"Why do you say that which you do not do?"* On this reading, Allah is saying: *the dearest of you to Me is he who fights in My cause.*

Some said instead that it was revealed about the gravity of fighting in battle — a man saying that he fought and endured the battle when he did not. Qatadah and Ad-Dahhak said this ayah was sent down to admonish some people who used to say that they killed, fought, stabbed and did such and such during battle, even though they did not do any of it. These are reported as different views of the occasion; each lands the same lesson from a different side — words about our own courage and commitment are held to account.

## Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: how far does the rebuke reach?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān works the phrase "what you do not do" carefully, and the result is useful, because most of us are somewhere in the middle of the scale it draws.

Apparently, it says, the phrase implies that one should not claim to do something he does not intend to do. From this it may be deduced that it is prohibited to make a commitment to a work while lacking the genuine intention to really do it, because this would be ostentation and a false commitment.

But the Companions in the occasion of revelation were plainly *not* in that category — their intention was genuine. From this we learn that the ayah also includes a second case: a person who commits to do something with true intention to do it, but relies solely on his own strength. That, it says, is not in keeping with his station of *'abdiyyah* — servitude before Allah. Its practical counsel is refreshingly plain: first of all, there is no need to make such a claim at all. If the occasion arises to do something, he may go ahead and do it. And if for some reason a person has to make a promise or claim, he may affirm it by saying "If Allah wills" — and in this way it would not be a boastful claim.

**The ruling it draws.** If a person claims that he will do something in future but has no intention to do it, that is a major sin (*kabīrah*) and a cause of incurring Allah's wrath — and it is to this situation that ayah 3, "It is severely hateful in Allah's sight," applies. But where one makes a claim to do something in future with real intention to do it, it is *makrūh* (reprehensible) and forbidden only if he makes the claim relying on his own strength and ability.

## An important boundary: a claim is not the same as preaching

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful to block a misuse of these ayat. They are related to false *daʿwā* — claims to do something in future without intention to do it. They are **not** about the situation of a preacher who invites others to a good he himself does not do. The rules of that situation are mentioned in other verses and ahadith — for example *"Do you bid others to righteousness while you ignore your own selves?"* (2:44), which puts to shame preachers who do not practise what they preach; its import is that when they preach to others, they should preach to themselves with greater force.

All this, it insists, does not imply that a person who has been lax in good deeds should abandon preaching to others, or that someone indulging in a sin should stop forbidding it. Performing a righteous deed is one form of virtue; urging others to perform it is another form of virtue in its own right. Abandoning the one does not mean abandoning the other — and it is possible that through the blessing of the preaching, the preacher himself may develop the ability to perform the deed, something Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says has been experienced widely and on a large scale.

What *is* required is honesty about the gap. If the deed belongs to the category of *wājib* (obligatory) or *sunnah mu'akkadah* (a strongly emphasised practice of the Prophet ﷺ), it is obligatory to continuously show remorse and regret at not practising it; and if the action belongs to the *mustahabbāt* (recommended acts), such remorse is itself *mustahab* — rewardable.

So the passage does not silence anyone. It asks for words matched by intention, humility about our own strength, and a heart that never gets comfortable with the distance between what it says and what it does.

## Ayah 4: the answer — ranks like a poured wall

Now the answer arrives: *"Verily, Allah loves those who fight in His cause in rows as if they were a solid structure."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states it plainly — the main subject of this surah, for which it was revealed, is to mention the dearest action in the sight of Allah, and this ayah states that it is jihād in Allah's way.

Look at what the wording carries.

**"In His cause" (*fī sabīlihi*).** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān specifies that the best row of battle in the sight of Allah is the one firmly established against Allah's enemies "to make Allah's word prevail." That is the purpose named in the ayah.

**"In rows" (*saffan*) — from which the surah takes its name.** Sa'id bin Jubayr said that before Allah's Messenger ﷺ began the battle against the enemy, he liked to line up his forces in rows; and in this surah, Allah teaches the believers to do the same. So the ayah is not only about courage; it is about *formation* — the ordered, shoulder-to-shoulder posture the Prophet ﷺ himself chose.

**"As if they were a solid structure" (*bunyān marsūs*).** The commentators dwell on this image. Sa'id bin Jubayr said it means its parts are firmly connected to each other, in rows for battle. Muqatil bin Hayyan said simply, "Firmly connected to each other." Ibn 'Abbas said: "They are like a firm structure that does not move, because its parts are cemented to each other." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān completes the picture: on account of the valour and unshaken determination of the mujāhidīn, the rank looks like a strong structure cemented with molten lead.

Feel the force of that comparison. What Ibn 'Abbas emphasises is that such a structure *does not move* — its parts are cemented to each other. That is what Allah loves: not a crowd of individually brave men, but men bound to one another.

And notice how ayah 4 answers ayat 2–3. What was corrected was a claim resting on personal strength. What is praised is a body of believers holding position together for a purpose that belongs to Allah — to make His word prevail. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that the surah then goes on to describe the jihād of the Prophets Mūsā and 'Īsā (peace be upon them) in Allah's cause, and how they suffered at the hands of their enemies, before directing the Muslims themselves to undertake jihād.

## Living it

- **Say less, and mean all of it.** Per Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, there is usually no need to announce the commitment at all; when the occasion arises, act.
- **When you must commit, say *in shā' Allah*** — affirming the promise by surrendering it to Allah's will, so that it is not a boastful claim.
- **Keep small promises.** The dates in the hadith recorded by Imam Ahmad and Abu Dawud were a small thing to everyone except the One who writes.
- **Do not claim a share of a struggle you did not carry** — the failing Qatadah and Ad-Dahhak described.
- **Keep calling to good even while you fall short of it**, and let the shortfall keep you in remorse rather than in silence.
- **Value being joined to others.** The ayah praises those whose ranks are firmly connected — as Ibn 'Abbas put it, a structure that does not move because its parts are cemented to each other.

passages.title: Moses and Jesus met with rejection
passages.tafsir:
Two great prophets stand before their own people, holding credentials those people cannot honestly deny — and are met with insult, evasion and mockery. Ayat 5–7 place Musa and 'Isa (peace be upon them) side by side, before the surah turns and calls the believers to their own struggle, and they console the Prophet ﷺ that what he was suffering was not new.

What binds the three ayat together is a single grim sequence: **truth is made plain → people reject it anyway → Allah leaves them in the darkness they chose.** Ayah 5 shows it with Musa, ayah 6 with 'Isa, and ayah 7 states the principle in the form of a question no one can answer: who could possibly be more wrong than this?

## Where this sits in the surah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that the surah's central subject had just been stated in ayah 4 — that Allah loves those who fight in His way in firm rows, "as if they were a solid edifice", a row so firmly established, and so marked by the valour and unshaken determination of those who hold it, that it looks like a strong structure cemented with molten lead. What follows in ayat 5–6 is a description of the struggles that Musa and 'Isa waged in Allah's cause and what they suffered at the hands of their enemies; only after that description does the surah direct the Muslims to their own struggle. In other words, before the Qur'an asks believers to hold the line, it shows them that prophets before them held it under fire. Maʿārif adds that these two stories carry many lessons, academic and practical, for anyone willing to look.

## Ayah 5: being hurt by people who know you are right

Ibn Kathir identifies the speaker precisely: Allah's servant and Messenger Musa, son of 'Imran, **the one to whom Allah spoke directly**. That detail matters. If anyone's standing was beyond dispute, it was his — and still his own people troubled him.

The ayah's complaint is simple and raw: *"Why do you annoy me while you know certainly that I am the Messenger of Allah to you?"* The real weight of it sits in the clause **wa qad taʿlamūn** — "when you know full well." Ibn Kathir explains the meaning as: *why do you annoy me even though you know my truth regarding the Message that I brought you?* This is not the resistance of the genuinely confused. It is hostility from people whose own knowledge convicts them. That is what makes it so bitter, and so blameworthy.

**Consolation for the Prophet ﷺ.** Ibn Kathir says plainly that this brings consolation to Allah's Messenger ﷺ for what the disbelievers among his people and others did to him — and that it orders him to be patient. He connects it to the Prophet's ﷺ own words: *"May Allah have mercy with Musa: he was annoyed more than this, yet he was patient."* (Ibn Kathir reports these words of the Prophet ﷺ here without naming a collection, so we take the teaching without attaching it to a named book.)

Read that as a believer and it reframes your own trials. The pattern is not personal; it is prophetic.

**A warning aimed at the believers themselves.** Ibn Kathir then draws out something easy to miss: by this ayah, believers are prohibited from harming or bothering the Prophet ﷺ in any way or form. He supports it with Allah's words, "O you who believe! Be not like those who annoyed Musa, but Allah cleared him of that which they alleged, and he was honorable before Allah" (33:69). The ayah is not only about ancient Israelites. It is a fence placed around the honour of the Messenger ﷺ for his own community.

## The most frightening line in the passage

Then comes: **fa-lammā zāghū azāgha Allāhu qulūbahum** — "so when they turned away, Allah turned their hearts away."

Ibn Kathir explains it exactly: when they turned away from following the guidance **even though they knew it**, Allah turned their hearts away from the guidance, and instead placed doubts, suspicion and failure in their hearts.

This is the Qur'an's law of the heart. Guidance that is refused is not left sitting there indefinitely. Ibn Kathir gathers other ayat that say the same thing:

- "And We shall turn their hearts and vision away, as they refused to believe therein for the first time, and We shall leave them in their trespass to wander blindly." (6:110)
- "And whoever contradicts and opposes the Messenger **after the right path has been shown clearly to him**, and follows other than the believers' way, We shall keep him in the path he has chosen, and enter him in Hell, what an evil destination it is!" (4:115)

In each case the condition is the same: knowledge came first. The closing of the heart is a consequence, not a whim. And so the ayah ends, "And Allah guides not the people who are rebellious" (*al-fāsiqīn*) — a phrase Ibn Kathir notes appears elsewhere in the Qur'an in exactly this sense (9:24).

**What to take from it:** never treat clarity casually. A truth you have understood and then shrugged off does not stay available to you forever.

## Ayah 6: 'Isa's two announcements

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads ayah 6 with great care. When 'Isa invited the Children of Israel to accept his prophethood and obey him, he mentioned **two things in particular**, and the ayah preserves both.

**First: *muṣaddiqan li-mā bayna yadayya min al-Tawrāh* — "confirming the Torah that came before me."** He was not announcing a new religion out of nowhere. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the point out: he said he was not a unique Prophet who came with unique teachings; his teachings were the same as those of the previous prophets, mentioned in the earlier celestial scriptures, and the same teachings would be imparted later by the Final Messenger ﷺ. The Torah is singled out — probably, Maʿārif suggests, because it was the latest scripture revealed to the Children of Israel; otherwise belief in the prophets embraces all of Allah's earlier scriptures. It also points out that although 'Isa's *sharīʿah* (revealed law) was an independent one, most of its rules conformed to the sacred laws of Musa and the Torah, with only a few laws changed.

Ibn Kathir catches the beautiful symmetry in it: the Torah conveyed the glad tidings of 'Isa's coming, and 'Isa's coming confirms the truth of the Torah. Each vouches for the other.

**Second: *mubashshiran bi-rasūlin ya'tī min baʿdī ismuhu Aḥmad* — "and giving glad tidings of a Messenger to come after me, whose name is Ahmad."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this too points out that the one coming after will teach what the prophets before taught, so it is the demand of reason and honesty to believe in him — and when he appears it becomes obligatory for them to embrace faith in him and obey him.

Ibn Kathir renders 'Isa's meaning in the first person: the Torah announced me, I confirm the Torah, and I convey the glad tidings of the Prophet who comes after me — the unlettered, Makkan, Arab Prophet and Messenger, Ahmad. He adds that 'Isa is the last and final Messenger from among the Children of Israel, who remained among them for a while conveying the good news of the one who was to come; and that after Muhammad ﷺ there will be no prophethood or Messengers.

## Why "Ahmad" and not "Muhammad"?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers a thoughtful answer. Both were names of the Final Messenger ﷺ, and he had some other names as well. But the name given in the Injil is *Ahmad* rather than *Muhammad* — perhaps because Muhammad had been a common name in Arabia since time immemorial, so there was a possibility that people might take the reference to be to someone else. *Ahmad*, by contrast, was an uncommon name in Arabia, and was exclusive to him ﷺ.

The Prophet ﷺ himself listed his names. Al-Bukhari collected in his *Sahih* from Jubayr bin Mutʿim, who said, "I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: 'I have names. I am Muhammad and Ahmad. I am Al-Māhī through whom Allah will eliminate disbelief. I am Al-Hāshir who will be the first to be resurrected, with the people being resurrected Hereafter. I am also Al-ʿĀqib'" — glossed in the narration as: there will be no Prophet after him. Ibn Kathir adds that Muslim also collected this hadith, from Az-Zuhri from Jubayr.

## Three signs that announced him ﷺ

Ibn Kathir gathers reports in which the Prophet ﷺ names the earliest announcements of his own coming — and the *bushrā* of 'Isa, the glad tidings he delivered, is always among them.

- Muhammad bin Ishaq recorded that Khalid bin Maʿdan said that some Companions asked, "O Allah's Messenger! Tell us about yourself." He said: "I am the (result of the) invocation made to Allah from my father Ibrahim and the good news 'Isa delivered. When my mother was pregnant with me, she had a dream in which she saw a light emanating from her that radiated the palaces of Busra in Ash-Sham." Ibn Kathir says this hadith has a good chain of narration, supported by other similar narrations.
- Imam Ahmad recorded that Al-ʿIrbād bin Sāriyah said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "I was written with Allah as the Last and Final of the Prophets, even when Adam was still clay. I will tell of the first good news announcing my advent: the (result of the) invocation to Allah made from my father Ibrahim, the good news 'Isa conveyed, and the dream that my mother saw. The mothers of all Prophets see similar dreams."
- Imam Ahmad recorded that Abu Umamah said, "I said, 'O Allah's Messenger! What was the first good news of your coming?'" and was given the same three-part answer: the invocation of Ibrahim, the good news 'Isa conveyed, and his mother's dream of a light emanating from her that filled the palaces of Ash-Sham.

So ayah 6 is not an isolated proof-text. It names one strand of a witness that runs from Ibrahim's supplication, through 'Isa's announcement, to the light his mother saw.

## The Negus recognises the prophecy

Ibn Kathir places here one of the most moving episodes of the seerah, recorded by Imam Ahmad from 'Abdullah bin Masʿūd. The Prophet ﷺ had sent eighty men to An-Najashi (the Negus) — among them Ibn Masʿūd himself, Jaʿfar bin Abi Talib, 'Abdullah bin ʿUrfutah, 'Uthman bin Mazʿūn and Abu Musa. The Quraysh sent 'Amr bin Al-ʿĀs and 'Umarah bin Al-Walid after them with a gift for the king.

'Amr and 'Umarah came to the king, prostrated before him, and stood to his right and left, saying: "Some of our cousins migrated to your land; they have abandoned us and our religion." The king asked where they were and summoned them. Jaʿfar said to the Muslims, "I will be your speaker today." When he entered he greeted the king but did not prostrate. They asked why. He said, "We only prostrate for Allah, the Exalted and Most Honoured." They asked why again. He said, "Allah has sent a Messenger to us from Him, who ordered us not to prostrate to anyone except Allah, the Exalted and Most Honoured. He also ordered us to perform prayer and give charity."

Then 'Amr bin Al-ʿĀs played what he thought was his winning card: "They contradict your creed about 'Isa, son of Maryam." The king asked, "What do you say about 'Isa and his mother Maryam?" Jaʿfar answered, "We only say what Allah said about him, that he is Allah's Word, a soul created by Allah and sent down to the honourable virgin who was not touched by a man nor bearing children before."

An-Najashi lifted a straw of wood and said: "O Ethiopians, monks and priests! By Allah, what they say about 'Isa is no more than what we say about him, not even a difference that equals this straw. You are welcomed among us, and greetings to him who sent you. **I bear witness that he is Allah's Messenger whom we read about in the Injil. He is the Prophet who 'Isa, son of Maryam, foretold the good news about his advent.** Live wherever you wish. By Allah, had I not been entrusted with the responsibilities of kingship, I would have gone to him, so that I could be honoured by carrying his slippers and his water for ablution."

He ordered that the gifts of the idolaters be returned to them. 'Abdullah bin Masʿūd soon returned and later fought at Badr; and when the Prophet ﷺ received the news that An-Najashi had died, he invoked Allah to forgive him.

Read against ayah 6, the story is almost a commentary in living form: a Christian king who knew what he read in his own scripture heard the prophecy of ayah 6, recognised the man it pointed to, and bore witness — while the people to whom the prophet had come said something very different.

## "This is plain magic"

That different response closes ayah 6: *fa-lammā jā'ahum bil-bayyināt qālū hādhā siḥrun mubīn* — "but when he came to them with clear proofs, they said: this is plain magic."

There is a question here about who "he" is. Ibn Kathir reports, according to Ibn Jurayj and Ibn Jarir, that this refers to **Ahmad** — the one who was anticipated, in accordance with the early Scriptures and the early generations. When the Prophet appeared bringing clear signs, the disbelievers and rejecters said: this is plain magic.

Note the shape of the accusation. They did not deny that something extraordinary was happening — *bayyināt*, clear proofs, are conceded in the very act of calling them magic. They only relabelled it so they would not have to follow it. That is the same disease as ayah 5: knowing, and turning away anyway.

## On the claim that the prophecy is not in the Injil

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān addresses the objection head-on. It is a known fact that the previously revealed Divine scriptures have been changed and distorted — the Jews and the Christians themselves have had to admit that the Torah and the Injil were subjected to change and distortion, so drastically that it is hardly possible to make out the original texts. Based on the distorted version of the Injil, Christians today challenge the Qur'anic account of the prophecy, asserting that no prophecy in the name of Ahmad is found in the Injil.

Maʿārif points the reader to a detailed answer: *Izhār-ul-Haqq* by Maulana Rahmatullah Kairanwi, a thorough analysis of Christianity and of the changes made to the Bible, which concludes that despite drastic changes in the present Biblical version, the prophecy about the Prophet Ahmad ﷺ is still available. The book was originally written in Arabic, with translations later appearing in Turkish and English (Christian missionaries attempted their utmost to destroy it); an Urdu translation was prepared more recently by Maulana Akbar 'Ali of Darul Uloom Karachi, with in-depth research into current versions of the Bible by Maulana Muhammad Taqi, published in three volumes — volume 3, pages 182–362, elaborating on the prophecies pertaining to the Prophet ﷺ with reference to currently published Bibles.

## Ayah 7: the question with no answer

**wa man aẓlamu mimman iftarā ʿalā Allāhi al-kadhib wa huwa yudʿā ilā al-Islām** — "And who does more wrong than the one who invents a lie against Allah, while he is being invited to Islam?"

Ibn Kathir's gloss is exact: none is more unjust than he who lies about Allah and calls upon rivals and associates partners with Him — **even while he is being invited to *tawḥīd* (the worship of Allah alone) and to worshipping Him sincerely.** The invitation is what makes the crime enormous. It is one thing to be lost with no one calling; it is another to be called, clearly and repeatedly, and to answer by inventing falsehood about the One calling you.

And so the ayah closes as ayah 5 did, with the same divine verdict in a slightly different key: ayah 5 ended, "And Allah guides not the people who are rebellious" (*al-fāsiqīn*); ayah 7 ends, "And Allah guides not the people who are wrongdoers" (*al-ẓālimīn*). Rebellion and wrongdoing bracket the passage — the same refusal named twice, and the same door closing on it twice.

## Living it

- **When people hurt you for telling the truth, remember Musa.** The Prophet ﷺ himself was consoled by this very ayah; Ibn Kathir says it brings him consolation and orders him to be patient.
- **Guard the honour of the Prophet ﷺ.** Ibn Kathir reads ayah 5 as prohibiting believers from harming or bothering him ﷺ in any way or form.
- **Act on what you know, quickly.** The passage's most sobering teaching is that turning away from guidance you already recognised invites Allah to turn the heart itself away.
- **Recognise the "plain magic" move in yourself.** Relabelling an inconvenient truth is easier than obeying it — and it is exactly what the rejecters did.

passages.title: Allah's light cannot be extinguished
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat answer a question the surah has been building toward: what actually happens when human beings set themselves against Allah's revelation? Ayah 8 shows the opposition — its intention, its method, and its total futility. Ayah 9 shows the reality standing opposite it: what Allah Himself has already set in motion. Held together, they make a single statement — the light is not defended by its followers, it is completed by its Owner.

## Where these ayat sit

Immediately before ayah 8 stands ayah 7: **"And who does more wrong than the one who invents a lie against Allah, while he is being invited to Islam? And Allah guides not the people who are wrongdoers."** Ibn Kathir explains its force: none is more unjust than he who lies about Allah and calls upon rivals and associates partners with Him — and does all this *while he is being invited* to tawhid (the pure oneness of Allah) and to worshipping Him sincerely.

The injustice is sharpened by the invitation. The truth is being held out to him with an open hand, and he answers by inventing falsehood about the One who is calling him.

That is the person ayah 8 then describes in action. Ayah 7 gives us his heart; ayah 8 gives us his hands — or rather, his mouth.

## Ayah 8: blowing at the sun

**يُرِيدُونَ لِيُطْفِـُٔوا نُورَ ٱللَّهِ بِأَفْوَٰهِهِمْ — "They intend to put out the Light of Allah with their mouths."**

Every word here is chosen to make the attempt look as small as it is.

**"They intend"** — the ayah begins with their *wanting*, not their doing. It reports an intention, a wish, a plan. It never gets as far as reporting a result, because there is no result to report.

**"With their mouths."** Consider what it actually means to put out a light with your mouth: you purse your lips and blow. That is the whole of it — a puff of breath. And that, says the ayah, is the sum of what the enemies of revelation bring against it. Ibn Kathir reads the phrase as an indication of their method: the disbelievers *will try to contradict the truth with falsehood*. Their weapon is talk — and behind the talk, the invented lie of ayah 7.

**"The Light of Allah."** Here the image turns devastating. Ibn Kathir writes:

> Their attempts are similar to one's attempt to extinguish the sun with his mouth, which is impossible. Likewise is the case of their attempt to extinguish truth.

Sit with that comparison for a moment. A man stands in open daylight and blows at the sun. He may keep at it as long as he likes; the sun is not dimmed by a single degree, because it was never within reach of his breath in the first place.

And notice what the comparison quietly settles. A candle *can* be blown out; the choice of the sun tells you what kind of light this is. It is not a light that human beings kindled and might therefore lose. It is *nūr Allāh* — Allah's own light, belonging to Him, sustained by Him, entirely outside the reach of anyone's mouth.

## "But Allah will bring His Light to perfection"

**وَٱللَّهُ مُتِمُّ نُورِهِ وَلَوْ كَرِهَ ٱلْكَٰفِرُونَ — "But Allah will bring His Light to perfection even though the disbelievers hate it."**

Against their *wanting*, Allah sets His *doing*. He describes Himself here with the word *mutimm* — the One who brings a thing to completion, who carries it all the way to its full state. The contrast is not merely that Allah will protect His light from them. It is that while they are busy blowing, He is busy *completing*. Their effort does not even register as an obstacle in the account; it is background noise to a work that is going forward regardless.

Then: **"even though the disbelievers hate it."** This clause is not there to taunt anyone. It is there to remove a particular illusion — the illusion that widespread hostility to the truth tells you something about the truth's prospects. Their hatred is real, and the ayah grants it. It simply denies that it is relevant to the outcome.

For a believer living among people who dislike his faith, this is a reordering of what counts as evidence. Opposition is not a sign that Allah's promise is faltering. The Qur'an named the opposition in the same breath as the promise.

## Ayah 9: the reason it cannot fail

**هُوَ ٱلَّذِىٓ أَرْسَلَ رَسُولَهُۥ بِٱلْهُدَىٰ وَدِينِ ٱلْحَقِّ لِيُظْهِرَهُۥ عَلَى ٱلدِّينِ كُلِّهِۦ وَلَوْ كَرِهَ ٱلْمُشْرِكُونَ — "He it is Who has sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth to make it victorious over all religions even though the idolators hate it."**

Ayah 9 supplies the ground of the guarantee in ayah 8. Why can this light not be blown out? Because of who lit it, and why.

**"He it is Who has sent."** The sentence begins with Allah — emphatically *He*, and no one else. The Messenger ﷺ did not appoint himself, and the message is not his project. That is precisely why no human effort can cancel it: what was not begun by people cannot be undone by people.

**"With guidance and the religion of truth."** Two things travel with him. *Hudā*, guidance — the light in its function of showing a person where to put his feet. And *dīn al-ḥaqq*, the religion of truth. Notice that the light of ayah 8 and the guidance of ayah 9 are one reality seen from two sides: from Allah's side it is His light; from ours it is our guidance.

**"To make it victorious over all religions."** The purpose is stated as the very reason for the sending. This is not a hope attached to the mission afterwards; it is the mission's declared end.

**"Even though the idolators hate it."** The refrain returns, with a change of word: ayah 8 said *al-kāfirūn*, those who reject; ayah 9 says *al-mushrikūn*, those who set up partners with Allah. That second word ties the passage back to ayah 7, where Ibn Kathir described exactly this man — calling upon rivals and associating partners with Allah while being invited to tawhid. The circle closes. The people who invent lies about Allah, the people who blow at His light, and the people whose hatred cannot stop His religion are one and the same people, described from three angles.

Ibn Kathir closes his comment by noting that he has already explained the meanings of similar ayat in his tafsir of Surah Baraʾah — a reminder that this is a settled and repeated Qur'anic declaration, not a one-off consolation offered in a hard moment.

## What the surah asks of the believer

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that this surah was revealed to name the action dearest to Allah in ayah 4: **"Surely Allah loves those who fight in His way in firm rows, as if they were a solid edifice"** — the row firmly established against Allah's enemies to make Allah's word prevail, which, through the valour and unshaken determination of the mujahidin, looks like a strong structure cemented with molten lead.

Maʿārif then notes the shape of the surah: this is followed by a description of the jihads which the Prophets Musa and ʿĪsā (peace be upon them) fought in Allah's cause, and how they suffered at the hands of the enemies — and only after that description are the Muslims directed to undertake jihad themselves.

So our two ayat land in a very particular place. They come after a long look at what earlier messengers endured while carrying this same message, and they come as the assurance underneath the summons that follows. Allah's word *will* prevail; the believer's part is to stand in the row.

## Living it

**Your task is the row, not the outcome.** Ayah 8 does not make the completion of Allah's light conditional on the believers holding the line; it states plainly that He will complete it. What the surah asks of you is what ayah 4 described — to stand firm, cemented like a solid structure, for the sake of Allah's word prevailing. The result rests with Allah; your place in the row is what rests with you.

**Recalibrate what noise means.** When mockery, distortion and organised hostility surround the faith, ayah 8 has already named that as the enemy's whole arsenal — mouths — and ayah 9 has already named the outcome. Anxiety about whether the truth will survive is anxiety about a question Allah has settled.

**Do not be on the wrong side of the blowing.** Ayah 7 is a warning before it is a description. The most unjust of people is not a distant villain; he is anyone who invents falsehood about Allah while the invitation to sincere worship is being extended to him. The safest response to a light you cannot put out is to walk in it.

passages.title: The saving bargain, and Allah's helpers
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat close Sūrah aṣ-Ṣaff by putting a single offer in front of the believer: Allah proposes a **trade** — you invest faith, wealth and effort in His cause, and He pays you rescue from a painful torment, forgiveness, Paradise, and, on top of all that, help and victory in this world. Ayah 14 then names the role this trade puts you in: to be **Allah's helpers**, exactly as the disciples of ʿĪsā (Jesus, peace be upon him) once were.

What holds the passage together is that it is the *answer* the whole sūrah has been building toward. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the main subject for which this sūrah was revealed is to name the action dearest to Allah — and that ayah 4 already identified it: those who fight in His way in firm rows, "as if they were a solid edifice," ranks so welded by the valour and unshaken determination of the fighters that they look like a strong structure cemented with molten lead. After that, the sūrah described the struggles of Mūsā and ʿĪsā (peace be upon them) in Allah's cause, and how they suffered at the hands of the enemies. Ayat 10–14 are where all of that turns and faces the reader: *now you.*

## The question the Companions were asking

Ibn Kathīr recalls a report from the Companion ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām that the Companions wanted to ask the Prophet ﷺ about the best actions with Allah, so that they could go and practise them. Allah sent down this sūrah — including this ayah — in reply. (Ibn Kathīr refers back to it here without naming a collection, so we take it as he gives it.)

That transforms how ayah 10 reads. It is Allah answering a question His servants were burning to ask — and He answers with an invitation rather than a command: **"Shall I guide you to a trade…?"**, addressed to *"O you who believe"*, people who have already said yes once and are now being shown what that yes is worth.

## Why "trade"?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the metaphor plainly: this ayah calls faith and struggle in Allah's way with one's wealth and life a *trade*, because when a man invests wealth in trade and works hard, he gains profit. So too here — when a man believes in Allah and invests his life and his wealth in His cause, he earns Allah's pleasure and the eternal blessings of the Hereafter.

And notice what kind of profit is being advertised. The trade is described as one that **saves you from a painful torment**. Ordinary commerce promises gain; this one promises *escape*. The reader is quietly being told that he is currently in danger, and that this is the way out. Ibn Kathīr sums it up: Allah then explained this great trade that will never fail — the trade that will earn a person what he wishes and save him from what he dislikes.

## The terms: what you put in (ayah 11)

Ayah 11 names two things, in this order:

1. **Faith in Allah and His Messenger ﷺ.** Belief comes first, because without it nothing else is a payment at all.
2. **Striving in the way of Allah with your wealth and your lives** — *jihād* here, as Ibn Kathīr renders it, meaning to strive hard and fight in the cause of Allah, spending both property and person.

Wealth is mentioned before lives. Most people are asked for the first long before they are ever asked for the second, and both are named because a cause carried by bodies alone, or by money alone, is only half-carried.

Then comes the appraisal: **"that will be better for you, if you but know."** Ibn Kathīr draws out exactly what the comparison is against — this is better than the trade of this life, and better than striving hard for it and amassing it. The phrase *"if you but know"* is the gentle sting in it. The profit is real; the reason people do not take the offer is not that the terms are bad but that they have not truly reckoned them.

## The payment: what Allah puts in (ayah 12)

Ibn Kathīr paraphrases Allah's side of the contract like this: *if you fulfil what I commanded you and guided you to, then I will forgive your sins and admit you into the Gardens of Paradise; in them you will have exalted residences and high positions.*

Look at the sequence in ayah 12, because it is the sequence of a life being repaired:

- **"He will forgive you your sins"** — the past is cleared first. Ayah 10 promised rescue from a painful torment; here is *how* the rescue happens. Not by the sins never having occurred, but by their being forgiven.
- **"and admit you into Gardens under which rivers flow"** — the general reward, the standing image of Paradise.
- **"and pleasant dwellings in ʿAdn Paradise"** — and then something more particular: not just admission to the Garden but *a home* in it. Ibn Kathīr's rendering glosses ʿAdn as "Eternal," and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān speaks of dwellings in the Gardens of Eternity with all sorts of luxuries and comforts — noting that the Prophet ﷺ himself gave an explanation of these "pleasant dwellings."
- **"that is indeed the great success"** — the verdict on the whole transaction. Anything else a person might call winning has just been silently demoted.

## The bonus you did not dare ask for (ayah 13)

Then ayah 13 adds something almost affectionate: **"And also another blessing which you love."** Ibn Kathīr's paraphrase: *I will grant you more favours that you like* — namely, **help from Allah and a near victory.**

Note that Allah does not merely say "and also victory." He names the believers' love for it before He names the gift, as if He knows perfectly well what they have been hoping for and is granting it before they voice it.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān handles the delicacy here well. Why single out a *worldly* blessing as "the one you love," when the Hereafter is obviously more beloved to a believer? Because, it says, this worldly blessing is dear to man since he is by nature prone to haste, as the Qurʼān says: *"and man is prone to haste"* (17:11). This does not imply that the blessings of the Hereafter are not dear to him — that love is obvious and assumed. It simply means that he naturally would love to have the blessings of this world as well; and Allah, knowing that about him, grants those too.

**What is the "near victory"?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the readings side by side:

- If *qarīb* ("near") is taken as the opposite of "in the Hereafter," it would include all the later Islamic conquests of Arab and non-Arab territories.
- If *qarīb* is taken in its normal sense, then it applies in the first instance to the conquest of Khaybar, and in the second instance to the Conquest of Makkah.

Ibn Kathīr reads it in this same direction: *and a near victory* means it will come sooner — the increased favour that is earned in this life and continues, becoming the delight of the Hereafter. And he is careful about who it is for: those who obey Allah and His Messenger ﷺ and support Allah and His religion.

He supports the promise with two other ayat that state the same law: *"O you who believe! If you help the cause of Allah, He will help you, and make your foothold firm"* (47:7), and *"Verily, Allah will help those who help His cause. Truly, Allah is All Strong, All-Wise"* (22:40). The help is not payment for a service Allah needed. It is what He grants to those who stand up for His dīn.

The passage then turns outward for one clause: **"and give glad tidings to the believers."** The one addressed is the Prophet ﷺ — go and tell them. The good news is not to be kept.

## "Be Allah's helpers" (ayah 14)

Ayah 14 converts the whole bargain into an identity. Ibn Kathīr: Allah orders His faithful servants to be Allah's supporters at all times, in all their statements and actions, sacrificing their selves and their wealth — and orders them to accept His call and His Messenger's call, just as the disciples answered ʿĪsā.

**Who were the ḥawāriyyūn?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the linguistic sense (citing Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī, which refers to Azharī): *ḥawāriyy* means a sincere friend who is free from any kind of adulteration — a loyalty with nothing mixed into it. That is why the people who believed in ʿĪsā are called by that name. They were twelve in number.

The scene is a moment of pressure, not of triumph. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān places the question at a time when ʿĪsā was being hurt by the enemies; he turned to his disciples and asked, **"Who are my supporters towards Allah?"** — meaning, as Ibn Kathīr explains it, *who will support me in conveying the message of Allah?* They answered: **"We are Allah's helpers"** — meaning, we will support you with regard to the message you have been sent with and will help you convey it. Twelve people volunteered and pledged their loyalty and helped him in preaching the religion. And Ibn Kathīr adds what came of that pledge: ʿĪsā sent the disciples to the various areas of ash-Shām to call the Greeks and the Israelites to Islam.

**The same question, asked again in Makkah.** This is the most striking thing Ibn Kathīr does with this ayah. He records that during the days of Ḥajj, Allah's Messenger ﷺ used to ask:

> "Who will support me in conveying the message of my Lord? Verily, the Quraysh have prevented me from conveying the message of my Lord."

The same words in the same predicament, centuries apart. And Allah answered: He raised up al-Aws and al-Khazraj to support the Prophet ﷺ — the residents of Madinah, who gave him their pledge and supported him, vowing to protect him from mankind and the jinn if he migrated to them. When he migrated to them with his Companions, they fulfilled their vow to Allah — and this, Ibn Kathīr says, is why Allah and His Messenger ﷺ called them **al-Anṣār, the Supporters**, until the name became synonymous with them. May Allah be pleased with them.

So ayah 14 is not asking for something unprecedented. It is asking the reader to take a place in a line that runs from the ḥawāriyyūn to the Anṣār. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presses the point: the blessed Companions of the Prophet ﷺ followed this example to the fullest extent, to a degree that stands unparalleled in the history of other communities — they incurred the enmity of Arab and non-Arab alike for the sake of Allah's religion, bore torture and persecution, and dedicated their lives, wealth and children to the cause. Eventually Allah granted them help and victory, and the territories of the enemies fell into their hands. Ayah 13's promise, kept in front of everyone's eyes.

## What happened to those who were asked before us

The rest of ayah 14 is sobering: **"Then a group of the Children of Israel believed and a group disbelieved."**

Ibn Kathīr describes the split. When ʿĪsā conveyed the message of his Lord to his people and the disciples supported him, a group of the Children of Israel believed and accepted the guidance he brought them. Another group was led astray: they rejected what he brought, denied his prophethood, and invented terrible lies about him and his mother. And a further group went to the opposite extreme, exaggerating over ʿĪsā until they elevated him above the level of prophethood that Allah had given him — dividing into sects and factions, some saying he was the son of Allah, some saying he was one in a trinity, some saying he was Allah Himself.

Both errors are failures of the same thing: taking the servant and messenger of Allah for what he was not.

Ibn Kathīr then cites a narration reported by Imām Abū Jaʿfar ibn Jarīr aṭ-Ṭabarī from Ibn ʿAbbās — and notes that an-Nasāʼī also collected this statement of Ibn ʿAbbās in his *Sunan*. In it, when Allah decided to raise ʿĪsā to heaven, he went to his companions — twelve men in the house — and told them that some of them would disbelieve in him after having believed in him. He then asked who would volunteer to be made to resemble him and be killed in his place, and be with him in his place. One of the youngest men present kept standing up to volunteer until ʿĪsā said, "Then it will be you." The appearance of ʿĪsā was cast upon that young man, while ʿĪsā himself was raised to heaven through an opening in the roof of the house; those who came looking for him arrested the one who appeared as him and killed him by crucifixion. The report then describes the followers dividing into three groups: al-Yaʿqūbiyyah (the Jacobites), an-Nasṭūriyyah (the Nestorians), and a third group who said that **Allah's servant and Messenger** remained with them as long as Allah willed and then Allah raised him up to Himself. That last group, the narration says, was the Muslim group. The two disbelieving groups collaborated against them and annihilated them, and Islam remained unjustly concealed — until Allah sent Muḥammad ﷺ.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports the same three-group account from Ibn ʿAbbās as al-Baghawī gives it (via Mazharī), and is careful to record a difference among the scholars. On that reading, "those who believed" in ayah 14 refers to the believers of the community of ʿĪsā, who came out on top over the disbelievers through the help and support of the Final Messenger ﷺ. Some scholars, however, hold that ʿĪsā's followers divided into two groups — those who made him Allah or Allah's son, and those who held him to be Allah's servant and Messenger — and that there was a war between them in which Allah granted victory to the believing faction. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the objection raised (from Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī): it is popularly understood that the institution of jihād did not exist in the religion of ʿĪsā, so it is inconceivable that those believers would have waged war — though it remains possible that the unbelieving side started it and the believers were forced to defend themselves, which would not fall under that category.

## "And they became uppermost"

**"So We gave power to those who believed against their enemies, and they became the victorious."** Ibn Kathīr: We gave them victory over the group that defied them, and they became uppermost over the disbelieving group — *when We sent Muḥammad ﷺ*, through the victory he gained over the religion of the disbelievers.

That is the resolution of the whole passage, and it reaches backwards and forwards at once. Backwards: the small, crushed group that got ʿĪsā right was not abandoned; their vindication simply arrived later than they would have chosen, in the mission of the Prophet ﷺ. Forwards: Ibn Kathīr concludes that the Ummah of Muḥammad ﷺ will always be prevalent on the truth until Allah's command comes, while they remain on this path — and that the last group of them will fight against the Dajjāl along with ʿĪsā, peace be upon him, according to ḥadīths in the authentic collections.

## Living it

Read as one unit, the passage asks for something very concrete.

**Take the offer seriously as an offer.** Allah framed it as commerce because commerce is a language we already reason in — cost, return, risk, timing. Ayah 11's *"if you but know"* implies the failure is almost always at the level of reckoning, not of information. Sit down and actually price the two trades against each other, as Ibn Kathīr does: this against the trade of this life and striving hard for it and amassing it.

**Pay in both currencies.** Ayah 11 names wealth and self. Whichever of the two you find easier to give is probably not the one being asked of you.

**Do not despise the worldly half of the promise.** Ayah 13 shows Allah granting help and victory in this life, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that this blessing is named as beloved because man is by nature prone to haste (17:11). Wanting to see the dīn helped and its people safe in your own lifetime is not a lower motive needing apology — it is a longing Allah Himself names and then answers.

**Answer the question when it is asked.** "Who are my supporters towards Allah?" was asked by ʿĪsā when the enemies were hurting him, and the same question was asked by the Prophet ﷺ when Quraysh had shut him out. In both cases the people who answered were ordinary and few, and in both cases their answer is what history remembers them by. Ibn Kathīr's framing of ayah 14 leaves no room for a passive believer: Allah orders His servants to be His supporters *at all times, in all their statements and actions*. Not only when it is dramatic, and not only when it is safe.

**And carry the good news.** Ayah 13 ends with an instruction to *tell* the believers. Part of helping Allah's cause is making sure the people beside you know what has been promised to them.
